We build on this idea by extending the conceptual framework where representations learned across models trained on the same data can be expressed as linear combinations of a \emph{universal} set of basis features. These basis features underlie the learning task itself and remain consistent across models, regardless of scale. From this framework, we propose the \textbf{Linear Representation Transferability (LRT)} Hypothesis -- that there exists an affine transformation between the representation spaces of different models. To test this hypothesis, we learn affine mappings between the hidden states of models of different sizes and evaluate whether steering vectors -- directions in hidden state space associated with specific model behaviors -- retain their semantic effect when transferred from small to large language models using the learned mappings. We find strong empirical evidence that such affine mappings can preserve steering behaviors. These findings suggest that representations learned by small models can be used to guide the behavior of large models, and that the LRT hypothesis may be a promising direction on understanding representation alignment across model scales.

papers.title: Analyzing (In)Abilities of SAEs via Formal Languages
papers.research_question: What are the abilities and inabilities of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) in interpreting language models, and how can we make them learn causally relevant features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes SAEs on formal languages, showing that while they can find interpretable features, these features often lack causal impact, and proposes a causal regularization method to incentivize learning of causally relevant features.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that causality should be a central target in SAE training, and the proposed method is a proof-of-concept step towards learning causally relevant features.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can identify interpretable latents corresponding to grammar features like depth and parts-of-speech.
SAE performance is highly sensitive to hyperparameters like regularization and normalization.
Interpretable features from standard SAEs do not necessarily have causal effects on model outputs.
The proposed causal regularization method can lead to SAE features with predictable causal impacts.
Top-k regularization outperforms L1 regularization in finding interpretable features.
papers.limitation:
The proposed method is a proof-of-concept and only tested on synthetic formal languages.
The method relies on the availability of correlated tokens for weak supervision, which may not always be present in real-world settings.
future_direction: Overcoming the limitation of relying on correlated tokens
Extending the method to real-world settings
papers.abstract: Autoencoders have been used for finding interpretable and disentangled features underlying neural network representations in both image and text domains. While the efficacy and pitfalls of such methods are well-studied in vision, there is a lack of corresponding results, both qualitative and quantitative, for the text domain. We aim to address this gap by training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on a synthetic testbed of formal languages. Specifically, we train SAEs on the hidden representations of models trained on formal languages (Dyck-2, Expr, and English PCFG) under a wide variety of hyperparameter settings, finding interpretable latents often emerge in the features learned by our SAEs. However, similar to vision, we find performance turns out to be highly sensitive to inductive biases of the training pipeline. Moreover, we show latents correlating to certain features of the input do not always induce a causal impact on model's computation. We thus argue that causality has to become a central target in SAE training: learning of causal features should be incentivized from the ground-up. Motivated by this, we propose and perform preliminary investigations for an approach that promotes learning of causally relevant features in our formal language setting.

papers.title: Steering Knowledge Selection Behaviours in LLMs via SAE-Based Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can we detect and resolve knowledge conflicts in LLMs by steering their internal activations at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SPARE, a training-free representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to identify and edit functional features in LLM activations, effectively steering knowledge selection behavior during inference.
papers.conclusion: SPARE offers an effective and efficient way to control knowledge selection in LLMs at inference time, without significant computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge conflicts can be detected in the residual stream of LLMs, especially in mid-layers.
SPARE effectively controls knowledge selection, outperforming existing representation engineering and contrastive decoding methods.
SPARE requires only a small set of SAE features (e.g., <0.05% for Gemma2-9B) for effective control.
The residual stream shows skewed representations when models use contextual knowledge compared to parametric knowledge.
Middle layers are more steerable for knowledge selection behavior.
papers.limitation:
Relies on pre-trained SAEs, which may not be available for all models.
Generalization to other types of tasks or conflicts (e.g., complex reasoning, multi-hop questions) is unclear.
Control is evaluated primarily in binary terms (contextual vs. parametric knowledge), while real-world decisions may require more nuance.
papers.abstract: Yu Zhao, Alessio Devoto, Giwon Hong, Xiaotang Du, Aryo Pradipta Gema, Hongru Wang, Xuanli He, Kam-Fai Wong, Pasquale Minervini. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: One-shot Optimized Steering Vector for Hallucination Mitigation for VLMs
papers.research_question: How to bridge the gap between input-dependent and input-independent steering for Vision Language Models (VLMs) to efficiently mitigate hallucinations and enhance safety?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes OSGA, a one-shot, input-independent steering framework that learns a generalizable steering vector from a single, automatically selected anchor datum to mitigate hallucinations and improve safety in VLMs without modifying model parameters.
papers.conclusion: OSGA is an effective and lightweight method for hallucination mitigation and safety enhancement in VLMs, offering a practical and scalable solution for reliable deployment.
papers.key_findings:
OSGA consistently outperforms baseline and state-of-the-art methods across multiple hallucination and safety benchmarks.
A single optimized steering vector generalizes well across unseen inputs and subtasks, demonstrating cross-instance transferability.
OSGA achieves a favorable trade-off between hallucination suppression (lower CHAIR scores) and content preservation (high recall).
The method improves both object-level and attribute-level hallucination mitigation, as shown on MME-Hall.
OSGA enhances safety performance, particularly in challenging categories like harmfulness and offensiveness on GOAT-Bench.
papers.limitation: For tasks requiring specific answer formats (e.g., Yes/No questions), the gains are relatively limited and overfitting can occur during optimization, leading the model to consistently respond with 'yes' or 'no'.
papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) achieve strong performance on multimodal tasks but still suffer from hallucination and safety-related failures that persist even at scale. Steering offers a lightweight technique to improve model performance. However, steering, whether input-dependent or input-independent, achieves a meaningful trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness. In this work, we observe that steering vectors can generalize across inputs when tasks share aligned semantic intent. Based on this insight, we propose \textbf{OSGA} (\textbf{O}ne-shot \textbf{S}teering with \textbf{G}enerative \textbf{A}nchor), an input-independent framework that improves model performance with a single optimization instance. OSGA first selects an informative sample via a variance-based data selection strategy and learns a single steering vector with a contrastive objective with generative anchor regularization. The resulting vector can be universally applied at a certain layer during inference time without modifying model parameters. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that a single OSGA-optimized steering vector consistently improves hallucination mitigation and safety enhancement with negligible overhead, highlighting one-shot steering as a practical and scalable solution for reliable VLMs.

papers.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
papers.research_question: Can transformer language models learn positional information without explicit positional encodings, and how do they do it?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without explicit positional encodings (NoPos) can learn implicit positional information and achieve competitive performance, and this ability is due to the causal attention mask.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models can learn positional information without explicit encodings, and this phenomenon is robust across settings but does not extend to masked language models, with the causal attention mechanism being the key factor.
papers.key_findings:
NoPos models achieve competitive perplexity compared to models with explicit positional encodings across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.
Probing experiments show that NoPos models learn an implicit notion of absolute positions in their hidden representations, similar to models with learned positional embeddings.
The success of NoPos models is unique to causal language models; masked language models fail to converge without positional encodings.
Shuffling the prefix tokens leads to a dramatic increase in loss, indicating that the model uses the learned positional information.
The causal attention mask is conjectured to allow the model to infer absolute positions by counting the number of attendable tokens.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models up to 1.3B parameters, and while the trend suggests the findings should hold for larger models, this is not tested.
NoPos models are always slightly worse than models with positional encodings, indicating that the inductive bias of positional encoding is important.
papers.abstract: Causal transformer language models (LMs), such as GPT-3, typically require some form of positional encoding, such as positional embeddings. However, we show that LMs without any explicit positional encoding are still competitive with standard models and that this phenomenon is robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.Probing experiments reveal that such models acquire an implicit notion of absolute positions throughout the network, effectively compensating for the missing information.We conjecture that causal attention enables the model to infer the number of predecessors that each token can attend to, thereby approximating its absolute position.Our findings indicate that causal LMs might derive positional awareness not only from the explicit positioning mechanism but also from the effects of the causal mask.

papers.title: Concept Sliders: LoRA Adaptors for Precise Control in Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we enable precise, interpretable control over attributes in image generations from diffusion models using low-rank parameter directions (concept sliders) derived from text or image pairs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Sliders, a method to create low-rank LoRA adaptors for diffusion models that enable precise, continuous, and composable control over image attributes with minimal interference.
papers.conclusion: Concept Sliders provide a simple and scalable paradigm for interpretable control of diffusion models, enabling continuous, single-pass adjustments and complex multi-concept manipulation beyond text-driven methods.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Sliders allow precise control over image attributes using text prompts or image pairs, with minimal entanglement.
Sliders are composable, enabling complex multi-attribute control by overlaying multiple low-rank directions.
The method can transfer latent directions from StyleGAN to diffusion models for nuanced visual control.
Concept Sliders can fix common distortions in generated images, such as improving hand realism and overall image quality.
A disentanglement objective and low-rank constraint are key to achieving targeted edits with reduced interference.
papers.limitation:
Some residual interference between edits remains, indicating a need for more careful selection of preservation directions.
The SDEdit inference technique helps preserve structure but can reduce edit intensity compared to full inference-time application.
papers.abstract: We present a method to create interpretable concept sliders that enable precise control over attributes in image generations from diffusion models. Our approach identifies a low-rank parameter direction corresponding to one concept while minimizing interference with other attributes. A slider is created using a small set of prompts or sample images; thus slider directions can be created for either textual or visual concepts. Concept Sliders are plug-and-play: they can be composed efficiently and continuously modulated, enabling precise control over image generation. In quantitative experiments comparing to previous editing techniques, our sliders exhibit stronger targeted edits with lower interference. We showcase sliders for weather, age, styles, and expressions, as well as slider compositions. We show how sliders can transfer latents from StyleGAN for intuitive editing of visual concepts for which textual description is difficult. We also find that our method can help address persistent quality issues in Stable Diffusion XL including repair of object deformations and fixing distorted hands. Our code, data, and trained sliders are available at https://sliders.baulab.info/

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformers Models
papers.research_question: How to interactively explore and understand what attention heads in transformer models have learned, specifically in BERT, by combining attention visualization with nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to explore and explain learned representations and attention mechanisms in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to reveal intelligible structure in learned representations of transformer models, demonstrated with BERT on the Wizard of Oz corpus.
papers.key_findings:
At early layers (e.g., layer 1), masked token embeddings show similarity to common tokens like punctuation and determinants, with no meaningful linguistic information encoded.
As layers progress, more part-of-speech information is added; by layer 6, BERT becomes confident that a masked token is a verb, refining this estimation in later layers.
Complex dependencies such as direct object (DOBJ) are detected in early-middle layers but rely on a combination of multiple attention heads, not individual heads.
Positional heads attend to succeeding or preceding tokens and encode linguistic information about the attended-to word, such as part-of-speech and dependency relations.
EXBERT enables interactive exploration of how attention heads contribute to encoding linguistic features in token embeddings through nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce powerful contextual representations that lead to improvements across many NLP tasks. Since these models are typically guided by a sequence of learned self attention mechanisms and may comprise undesired inductive biases, it is paramount to be able to explore what the attention has learned. While static analyses of these models lead to targeted insights, interactive tools are more dynamic and can help humans better gain an intuition for the model-internal reasoning process. We present exBERT, an interactive tool named after the popular BERT language model, that provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations by matching a human-specified input to similar contexts in a large annotated dataset. By aggregating the annotations of the matching similar contexts, exBERT helps intuitively explain what each attention-head has learned.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Measuring the Mixing of Contextual Information in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How is contextual information mixed across the Transformer architecture, and how can this mixing be measured to provide faithful explanations for model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ALTI, an interpretability method that measures token-to-token interactions within each Transformer layer and aggregates them to provide input attribution scores, demonstrating more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: ALTI is a powerful interpretability method that quantifies the mixing of information in the Transformer, providing faithful input attributions and opening new possibilities for studying contextual information aggregation.
papers.key_findings:
ALTI outperforms gradient-based and other attribution methods in faithfulness metrics (comprehensiveness and sufficiency) across multiple models and datasets.
ALTI provides more robust interpretations across models with identical architecture but different random initializations, as measured by Jaccard similarity and Spearman correlation.
Using ℓ1 norm for measuring token contributions in ALTI is beneficial due to the anisotropic nature of Transformer representations and the presence of outlier dimensions.
The proposed layer-wise contribution measurement (based on distance to the output) significantly improves upon a previous norm-based approach.
Including the second layer normalization (from the feed-forward module) in the analysis has negligible impact on the faithfulness of the interpretations.
papers.limitation:
ALTI does not consider the classifier on top of the Transformer and therefore does not provide explanations for each of the output classes, unlike gradient-based methods.
Faithfulness is evaluated only via sufficiency and comprehensiveness metrics.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture aggregates input information through the self-attention mechanism, but there is no clear understanding of how this information is mixed across the entire model. Additionally, recent works have demonstrated that attention weights alone are not enough to describe the flow of information. In this paper, we consider the whole attention block --multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization-- and define a metric to measure token-to-token interactions within each layer. Then, we aggregate layer-wise interpretations to provide input attribution scores for model predictions. Experimentally, we show that our method, ALTI (Aggregation of Layer-wise Token-to-token Interactions), provides more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.

papers.title: GAN Dissection: Visualizing and Understanding Generative Adversarial Networks
papers.research_question: How does a GAN represent our visual world internally? What causes the artifacts in GAN results? How do architectural choices affect GAN learning?
papers.core_contribution: Presents an analytic framework to visualize and understand GANs at the unit, object, and scene levels, identifying interpretable units that correspond to object concepts and measuring their causal effects through interventions.
papers.conclusion: GANs learn interpretable and causally relevant units for objects, and the proposed dissection and intervention framework enables understanding, debugging, and manipulating GAN models.
papers.key_findings:
GANs develop interpretable units (channels) in their convolutional layers that correlate with object concepts and object parts.
These units have causal effects on object generation; ablating them removes objects, and inserting them adds objects.
The framework can diagnose and improve GANs by locating and ablating artifact-causing units, improving output quality.
Representations vary across layers: early layers have few interpretable units, middle layers have object units, and later layers have texture/color units.
Different GAN architectures (e.g., with minibatch stddev or pixelwise normalization) learn different numbers and types of interpretable units.
papers.limitation:
The method is not designed to compare the quality of GANs to one another, and it is not a replacement for metrics like FID.
The current method cannot fully explain why some interventions are suppressed (e.g., why a door cannot be inserted in the sky) or how the GAN suppresses signals in later layers.
future_direction: Further work to understand the relationships between layers of a GAN.
Applying the method to other generative models such as VAEs and RealNVP.
papers.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have recently achieved impressive results for many real-world applications, and many GAN variants have emerged with improvements in sample quality and training stability. However, they have not been well visualized or understood. How does a GAN represent our visual world internally? What causes the artifacts in GAN results? How do architectural choices affect GAN learning? Answering such questions could enable us to develop new insights and better models. In this work, we present an analytic framework to visualize and understand GANs at the unit-, object-, and scene-level. We first identify a group of interpretable units that are closely related to object concepts using a segmentation-based network dissection method. Then, we quantify the causal effect of interpretable units by measuring the ability of interventions to control objects in the output. We examine the contextual relationship between these units and their surroundings by inserting the discovered object concepts into new images. We show several practical applications enabled by our framework, from comparing internal representations across different layers, models, and datasets, to improving GANs by locating and removing artifact-causing units, to interactively manipulating objects in a scene. We provide open source interpretation tools to help researchers and practitioners better understand their GAN models.

papers.title: Inverting Supervised Representations with Autoregressive Neural Density Models
papers.research_question: How can we invert supervised representations to gain insights into the invariances learned by models and to estimate the mutual information between inputs and intermediate representations?
papers.core_contribution: Presents a method for inverting supervised representations using autoregressive neural density models, enabling visualization of model invariances and estimation of mutual information between inputs and intermediate representations.
papers.conclusion: The method facilitates visualization of model invariances and provides a scalable quantitative estimate of the amount of information preserved by a network.
papers.key_findings:
Mutual information between inputs and network layers decreases through successive layers, with the biggest reduction between CONV1 and CONV2.
Global pooling induces translation invariance in convolutional networks, while preserving style and rotation information.
Mutual information initially increases and then decreases over the course of training, supporting the information bottleneck theory.
Inversion models provide better calibration of variability compared to SGAN and nearest neighbor methods.
The method allows analysis of architectural choices by revealing invariances learned by different network architectures.
papers.limitation: Density estimation is challenging in higher dimensions, and it is not known how well a given model represents the true density.
future_direction: Improving the method as neural density models improve to achieve tighter mutual information bounds and more representative samples.
papers.abstract: We present a method for feature interpretation that makes use of recent advances in autoregressive density estimation models to invert model representations. We train generative inversion models to express a distribution over input features conditioned on intermediate model representations. Insights into the invariances learned by supervised models can be gained by viewing samples from these inversion models. In addition, we can use these inversion models to estimate the mutual information between a model’s inputs and its intermediate representations, thus quantifying the amount of information preserved by the network at different stages. Using this method we examine the types of information preserved at different layers of convolutional neural networks, and explore the invariances induced by different architectural choices. Finally we show that the mutual information between inputs and network layers initially increases and then decreases over the course of training, supporting recent work by Shwartz-Ziv and Tishby (2017) on the information bottleneck theory of deep learning.

papers.title: What Do Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn?
papers.research_question: What do self-supervised vision transformers learn? Specifically, how and why contrastive learning (CL) and masked image modeling (MIM) differ in their representations and downstream task performance.
papers.core_contribution: CL and MIM learn complementary representations: CL captures global shape information but suffers from attention collapse, while MIM captures local texture information and preserves diversity. A simple linear combination of both losses can outperform each individually.
papers.conclusion: CL and MIM have opposing properties and are complementary; combining them can improve performance, and even a simple harmonization method shows benefits.
papers.key_findings:
CL trains self-attentions to capture global patterns and object shapes, but leads to attention collapse into homogeneity, reducing representation diversity.
MIM focuses on local patterns and textures, preserving token-level diversity and excelling in fine-tuning and dense prediction tasks.
CL utilizes low-frequency signals (shape-biased), while MIM utilizes high-frequency signals (texture-biased).
CL plays a crucial role in later layers, while MIM is important in early layers.
A simple linear combination of CL and MIM objectives can leverage the advantages of both methods, improving performance in linear probing and fine-tuning.
future_direction: Exploring better ways to combine CL and MIM than linear combination, such as applying CL in later layers and MIM in early layers.
Extending findings to multi-stage Vision Transformers like PiT and Swin.
Enhancing individual properties of CL and MIM to improve shape or texture learning.
papers.abstract: We present a comparative study on how and why contrastive learning (CL) and masked image modeling (MIM) differ in their representations and in their performance of downstream tasks. In particular, we demonstrate that self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) have the following properties: (1) CL trains self-attentions to capture longer-range global patterns than MIM, such as the shape of an object, especially in the later layers of the ViT architecture. This CL property helps ViTs linearly separate images in their representation spaces. However, it also makes the self-attentions collapse into homogeneity for all query tokens and heads. Such homogeneity of self-attention reduces the diversity of representations, worsening scalability and dense prediction performance. (2) CL utilizes the low-frequency signals of the representations, but MIM utilizes high-frequencies. Since low- and high-frequency information respectively represent shapes and textures, CL is more shape-oriented and MIM more texture-oriented. (3) CL plays a crucial role in the later layers, while MIM mainly focuses on the early layers. Upon these analyses, we find that CL and MIM can complement each other and observe that even the simplest harmonization can help leverage the advantages of both methods. The code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/cl-vs-mim.

papers.title: On Efficient Transformer-Based Image Pre-training for Low-Level Vision
papers.research_question: How does pre-training act in image processing systems (low-level vision tasks) and what are effective pre-training strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes how pre-training affects internal representations in low-level vision tasks and finds that multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than other strategies.
papers.conclusion: Pre-training plays a central role in developing stronger intermediate representations by incorporating more local information, and its effect is task-specific. Multi-related-task pre-training is highly effective and data-efficient for low-level vision.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-training introduces more local information to higher layers in super-resolution and deraining, yielding significant performance gains, while it hardly affects internal feature representations in denoising, resulting in limited gains.
Multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than single-task or multi-unrelated-task pre-training.
Larger model capacities generally obtain more improvements from pre-training.
Transformers benefit more from pre-training than CNNs, providing higher performance baselines with fewer parameters.
The internal representations of SR and deraining models show clear stages (more local in early layers, more global in higher layers), while denoising models present a relatively uniform structure filled with local information.
papers.limitation:
The study mainly investigates pre-training on synthesized data; future research should explore real-world settings and more tasks, extended to video processing.
The encoder-decoder design uses a fixed downsampling strategy, which may not be optimal for all degradation levels; adaptive downsampling could be better.
future_direction: Explore pre-training in real-world settings and more tasks.
Extend the study to video processing.
Investigate adaptive downsampling based on degradation degrees.
papers.abstract: Pre-training has marked numerous state of the arts in high-level computer vision, while few attempts have ever been made to investigate how pre-training acts in image processing systems. In this paper, we tailor transformer-based pre-training regimes that boost various low-level tasks. To comprehensively diagnose the influence of pre-training, we design a whole set of principled evaluation tools that uncover its effects on internal representations. The observations demonstrate that pre-training plays strikingly different roles in low-level tasks. For example, pre-training introduces more local information to higher layers in super-resolution (SR), yielding significant performance gains, while pre-training hardly affects internal feature representations in denoising, resulting in limited gains. Further, we explore different methods of pre-training, revealing that multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than other alternatives. Finally, we extend our study to varying data scales and model sizes, as well as comparisons between transformers and CNNs-based architectures. Based on the study, we successfully develop state-of-the-art models for multiple low-level tasks. Code is released at https://github.com/fenglinglwb/EDT.

papers.title: Fine-Grained control over Music Generation with Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How to achieve fine-grained control over music generation through inference-time interventions on a music transformer model.
papers.core_contribution: A method for fine-grained control over music generation through inference-time interventions on MusicGen, using activation steering on the residual stream and attention outputs.
papers.conclusion: Fine-grained control over genre fusion and instrument transfer is achieved with a lightweight intervention method, extending activation engineering techniques to music generation.
papers.key_findings:
Musical concepts such as pitch, instruments, and genres are linearly represented in MusicGen's activations.
Linear probes trained with mean-squared error loss provide better steering vectors compared to cross-entropy loss.
Activation steering enables timbre transfer, style transfer, and genre fusion in music generation.
Interventions on the residual stream and attention outputs are effective for controlling generation.
papers.limitation: Reliable methods to determine the steering strength are not established and require hyper-parameter search.
future_direction: Identifying reliable methods to determine steering strength.
Gaining insights into superposition phenomena in activations for more generalizable interventions.
papers.abstract: We present a method for fine-grained control over music generation through inference-time interventions on an autoregressive generative music transformer called MusicGen. Our approach enables timbre transfer, style transfer, and genre fusion by steering the residual stream using weights of linear probes trained on it, or by steering the attention layer activations in a similar manner. We observe that modelling this as a regression task provides improved performance, hypothesizing that the mean-squared-error better preserve meaningful directional information in the activation space. Combined with the global conditioning offered by text prompts in MusicGen, our method provides both global and local control over music generation. Audio samples illustrating our method are available at our demo page.

papers.title: Steerable Chatbots: Personalizing LLMs with Preference-Based Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be used to personalize LLM outputs to align with user preferences, and how do users prefer to interact with such steerable chatbot interfaces?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that preference-based activation steering is an effective, lightweight method for personalizing LLM outputs to user preferences and presents three interactive chatbot interface designs (SELECT, CALIBRATE, LEARN) that allow users to control this steering.
papers.conclusion: Preference-based activation steering is a promising method for personalizing LLMs, and exposing the steering parameter through different interfaces can cater to diverse user preferences for control and interaction.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering effectively controls the intensity and direction of preference expressions in LLM outputs across multiple models.
Steering can be combined with natural language prompting, allowing users to provide contextual preferences on top of a steered latent preference.
In a user study, steered chatbots (SELECT, CALIBRATE) generated outputs that correlated significantly better with users' true underlying preferences than a prompting-only baseline.
Users exhibited heterogeneous preferences for the different interface designs (SELECT, CALIBRATE, LEARN), with each design appealing to different values around control, usability, and transparency.
The sentiment-based learning algorithm used in the LEARN interface was less robust at capturing user preferences compared to direct control (SELECT) or calibration (CALIBRATE).
papers.limitation:
The user study had a small sample size (n=14), limiting the generalizability of the subjective findings.
The sentiment-based learning algorithm in the LEARN interface was not robust enough to adapt to diverse user feedback.
future_direction: Improving the learning algorithm for the LEARN interface to better capture user intent.
Exploring the application of steering to a broader set of preferences and tasks.
Investigating the long-term effects of using steerable chatbots on user trust and satisfaction.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) improve in their capacity to serve as personal AI assistants, their ability to output uniquely tailored, personalized responses that align with the soft preferences of their users is essential for enhancing user satisfaction and retention. However, untrained lay users have poor prompt specification abilities and often struggle with conveying their latent preferences to AI assistants. To address this, we leverage activation steering to guide LLMs to align with interpretable preference dimensions during inference. In contrast to memory-based personalization methods that require longer user history, steering is extremely lightweight and can be easily controlled by the user via an linear strength factor. We embed steering into three different interactive chatbot interfaces and conduct a within-subjects user study (n=14) to investigate how end users prefer to personalize their conversations. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of preference-based steering for aligning real-world conversations with hidden user preferences, and highlight further insights on how diverse values around control, usability, and transparency lead users to prefer different interfaces.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Understanding Unreliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models: Geometric Predictors and the Limits of Linear Approximations
papers.research_question: What are the underlying factors in model activation patterns that contribute to the observed variability in CAA steering vector reliability across different datasets and target behaviors? Can the training process of CAA steering vectors be modified to produce more consistently reliable control over language model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The thesis demonstrates that steering vector unreliability is caused by a mismatch between the simple linear function class of CAA and the often non-linear latent target behavior representations. It identifies geometric predictors (directional agreement and separability) of steering reliability.
papers.conclusion: The reliability of CAA steering vectors is predictable from the geometry of the training activations. High directional agreement and clear separability along the difference-of-means line are key indicators of steerability.
papers.key_findings:
Higher cosine similarity (directional agreement) between training activation differences predicts more reliable steering.
Better separability of positive and negative activations along the steering direction predicts more reliable steering.
Steering vectors trained on different prompt variations are directionally distinct but perform similarly and have correlated efficacy across datasets.
Steering vector unreliability stems from the linear function class being too restrictive to approximate non-linear latent behavior representations.
Prompt types that leverage in-context learning (e.g., instructions, few-shot) lead to higher directional agreement and faster steering vector convergence.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to one model (Llama 2-7B-Chat) and one family of steering methods (CAA).
The analysis is restricted to binary classification tasks and may not generalize to more complex behaviors.
The study does not investigate the impact of model scale or architecture.
future_direction: Developing more robust steering methods that explicitly account for non-linear latent behavior representations.
Extending the analysis to more models, architectures, and a broader range of behaviors.
Investigating the impact of model scale on steering reliability.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a lightweight method for controlling language model behavior by adding a learned bias to the activations at inference time. Although effective on average, steering effect sizes vary across samples and are unreliable for many target behaviors. In my thesis, I investigate why steering reliability differs across behaviors and how it is impacted by steering vector training data. First, I find that higher cosine similarity between training activation differences predicts more reliable steering. Second, I observe that behavior datasets where positive and negative activations are better separated along the steering direction are more reliably steerable. Finally, steering vectors trained on different prompt variations are directionally distinct, yet perform similarly well and exhibit correlated efficacy across datasets. My findings suggest that steering vectors are unreliable when the latent target behavior representation is not effectively approximated by the linear steering direction. Taken together, these insights offer a practical diagnostic for steering unreliability and motivate the development of more robust steering methods that explicitly account for non-linear latent behavior representations.

papers.title: Steering Large Language Model Activations in Sparse Spaces
papers.research_question: How can we steer large language model behavior in a more interpretable and fine-grained way by leveraging sparse representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Steering (SAS), a method that uses sparse autoencoders to extract interpretable steering vectors from contrastive prompt pairs, enabling precise and modular control over LLM behavior during inference.
papers.conclusion: SAS provides an effective framework for steering LLM behavior in sparse spaces, offering improved interpretability and fine-grained control compared to dense activation steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAS vectors enable nuanced behavioral modulation and finer-grained control over LLM outputs.
Scaling sparse autoencoders (increasing dictionary size) improves the monosemanticity of the extracted SAS vectors.
Sparse representations allow for modular control, enabling fine-grained behaviors to be composed simultaneously.
papers.abstract: A key challenge in AI alignment is guiding large language models (LLMs) to follow desired behaviors at test time. Activation steering, which modifies internal model activations during inference, offers a potential solution. However, prior work in dense activation spaces struggles with superposition, wherein multiple features become entangled, limiting interpretability and precise control. In contrast, sparse representations provide an untapped opportunity for more interpretable behavior modulation. In this work, we introduce sparse activation steering (SAS), a method that leverages sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steer LLM behavior in sparse spaces. By isolating behavior-specific features through a contrastive prompt-pairing approach, we define a set of features that can selectively reinforce or suppress behaviors. Experiments on Gemma 2 LLMs show that SAS vectors enable nuanced behavioral modulation and finer-grained control. Furthermore, scaling SAEs improves monosemanticity of SAS vectors, suggesting more reliable and interpretable interventions.

papers.title: A Comparative Analysis of Sparse Autoencoder and Activation Difference in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve language model steering by selecting the most relevant sparse autoencoder (SAE) features and applying a token-wise decaying steering strategy to avoid degenerate outputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a method to select the most relevant SAE feature for steering and introduces a token-wise decaying steering strategy, which improves stability and performance in mathematical reasoning and instruction following tasks.
papers.conclusion: Decaying SAE steering is an effective method for controlling language model behavior, providing a more interpretable alternative to mean activation difference, especially in mathematical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE steering with a single relevant feature and decaying strategy outperforms constant steering and mean activation difference in math reasoning.
SAE steering can elicit step-by-step mathematical reasoning without few-shot prompts.
In instruction following, SAE steering matches the performance of mean activation difference.
The proposed feature selection method effectively removes redundant SAE features.
Decaying steering avoids degenerate outputs such as repetitive words.
papers.limitation:
The proposed method struggles with word inclusion tasks, as no single SAE feature reliably encodes lexical constraints.
The explanations from Neuronpedia are not guaranteed to be precise.
future_direction: Finer-grained SAE combinations for language proximity cases.
Multilingual-aware alignment strategies for steering.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for language model steering. Prior work has explored top-k SAE latents for steering, but we observe that many dimensions among the top-k latents capture non-semantic features such as punctuation rather than semantic attributes like instructions. To address this, we propose focusing on a single, most relevant SAE latent (top-1), eliminating redundant features. We further identify a limitation in constant SAE steering, which often produces degenerate outputs such as repetitive single words. To mitigate this, we introduce a token-wise decaying steering strategy, enabling more faithful comparisons with mean activation difference baselines. Empirically, we show that steering an SAE latent associated with reasoning reliably elicits step-by-step mathematical reasoning and enhances inference quality, functionally resembling the effect of appending a guiding token. Our results demonstrate that SAEs outperform mean activation difference methods on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and match their performance on IF-Eval.

papers.title: A gentle push funziona benissimo: making instructed models in Italian via contrastive activation steering
papers.research_question: Can activation steering be used to adapt models to Italian language tasks as an alternative to fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can adapt models to Italian language tasks with less data and computational cost than fine-tuning, achieving comparable or better performance and higher language consistency.
papers.conclusion: Steering is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for language adaptation, especially when using translated data, and it preserves existing knowledge without catastrophic forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Italian steering can be successfully applied to different models, including Llama 3 and Phi 3.
Steering achieves performances comparable to or better than fine-tuned models on Italian benchmarks.
Steering yields higher quality and consistency in Italian generations compared to fine-tuning.
Steering does not suffer from catastrophic forgetting, unlike fine-tuning.
Steering is more effective on older models (e.g., Llama 2) than on newer models (e.g., Llama 3) that already have high Italian performance.
papers.limitation: Steering has a theoretical upper bound because it does not inject new knowledge into the model, only enhances existing capabilities.
future_direction: Using native examples for the steering procedure.
Exploring style-specific steering.
papers.abstract: Adapting models to a language that was only partially present in the pre-training data requires fine-tuning, which is expensive in terms of both data and computational resources. As an alternative to fine-tuning, we explore the potential of activation steering-based techniques to enhance model performance on Italian tasks. Through our experiments we show that Italian steering (i) can be successfully applied to different models, (ii) achieves performances comparable to, or even better than, fine-tuned models for Italian, and (iii) yields higher quality and consistency in Italian generations. We also discuss the utility of steering and fine-tuning in the contemporary LLM landscape where models are anyway getting high Italian performances even if not explicitly trained in this language.

papers.title: Emergent World Models and Latent Variable Estimation in Chess-Playing Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models form robust world models and learn to estimate latent variables when trained on real, non-synthetic data, specifically chess games?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a language model trained on real chess games learns linear internal representations of the board state and player skill, and that these representations can be used to causally intervene on the model's behavior, editing its internal state and modifying its playing ability.
papers.conclusion: Language models trained on next-token prediction can develop world models and estimate latent variables even from real, non-synthetic data, and these representations are causally relevant to model behavior, as shown through successful interventions in the constrained domain of chess.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns a linear internal representation of the chess board state, which can be extracted with high accuracy using linear probes.
The model learns to estimate the Elo rating (player skill) as a latent variable to improve next-character prediction, and this representation can also be probed.
Interventions using vectors derived from linear probes or contrastive activations can successfully edit the model's internal board state, causing it to play legal moves under a hypothetical modified board.
Adding a skill vector derived from contrastive activations to the model's MLP bias term can increase the model's win rate against Stockfish by up to 2.6 times, while subtracting it decreases performance.
The board state representation peaks in accuracy in the middle layers of the model, while the skill representation peaks in the final layers, suggesting parallel computation of board state and skill estimation.
papers.limitation:
The board state intervention success rate is 92%, indicating potential for improved intervention strategies.
Interventions can have unintended side effects, making the positions of other pieces less distinct.
The model's maximum input length of 1,023 characters limits the number of turns in a game.
Chess is a well-defined, rule-based system that does not capture the complexity and ambiguity present in less structured environments like natural language.
future_direction: Improving intervention strategies
Applying the techniques to natural language domains
Using the methods for applications like detecting and reducing hallucinations in LLMs
papers.abstract: Language models have shown unprecedented capabilities, sparking debate over the source of their performance. Is it merely the outcome of learning syntactic patterns and surface level statistics, or do they extract semantics and a world model from the text? Prior work by Li et al. investigated this by training a GPT model on synthetic, randomly generated Othello games and found that the model learned an internal representation of the board state. We extend this work into the more complex domain of chess, training on real games and investigating our model's internal representations using linear probes and contrastive activations. The model is given no a priori knowledge of the game and is solely trained on next character prediction, yet we find evidence of internal representations of board state. We validate these internal representations by using them to make interventions on the model's activations and edit its internal board state. Unlike Li et al's prior synthetic dataset approach, our analysis finds that the model also learns to estimate latent variables like player skill to better predict the next character. We derive a player skill vector and add it to the model, improving the model's win rate by up to 2.6 times.

papers.title: Interpretable and Steerable Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the interpretability and steerability of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) by incorporating user-specified concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE), a framework that prunes low-utility SAE neurons and augments the latent space with a concept bottleneck aligned to user-defined concepts, improving interpretability and steerability.
papers.conclusion: CB-SAE unifies sparse autoencoders with concept bottleneck models, enabling robust interpretation and control of vision representations across modalities and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE neurons have low interpretability or steerability, rendering them ineffective for downstream use.
SAEs often fail to represent user-specified concepts, limiting their practical utility.
CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% over SAE baselines across LVLMs and image generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) promise a unified approach for mechanistic interpretability, concept discovery, and model steering in LLMs and LVLMs. However, realizing this potential requires that the learned features be both interpretable and steerable. To that end, we introduce two new computationally inexpensive interpretability and steerability metrics and conduct a systematic analysis on LVLMs. Our analysis uncovers two observations; (i) a majority of SAE neurons exhibit either low interpretability or low steerability or both, rendering them ineffective for downstream use; and (ii) due to the unsupervised nature of SAEs, user-desired concepts are often absent in the learned dictionary, thus limiting their practical utility. To address these limitations, we propose Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE) - a novel post-hoc framework that prunes low-utility neurons and augments the latent space with a lightweight concept bottleneck aligned to a user-defined concept set. The resulting CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% across LVLMs and image generation tasks. We will make our code and model weights available.

papers.title: The Hidden Life of Tokens: Reducing Hallucination of Large Vision-Language Models via Visual Information Steering
papers.research_question: How does hallucination emerge and propagate internally during generation in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), and how can it be reduced via inference-time intervention?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces VISTA, a training-free inference-time intervention framework that reduces hallucination in LVLMs by reinforcing visual information in the activation space (via Visual Steering Vector) and leveraging early-layer semantic information (via Self-Logits Augmentation).
papers.conclusion: VISTA effectively reduces hallucination in LVLMs while preserving generation quality, establishing visual information steering as a promising direction for enhancing the reliability of multimodal AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Gradual visual information loss: visually grounded tokens become less favored as generation progresses.
Early excitation: semantically meaningful tokens achieve peak activation in layers earlier than the final layer.
Hidden genuine information: visually grounded tokens not decoded still retain relatively high rankings during inference.
VISTA reduces hallucination by about 40% on average in open-ended generation tasks.
VISTA outperforms existing methods across four benchmarks, four architectures, and three decoding strategies.
papers.limitation:
Optimal hyperparameter settings may vary across different architectures.
The effectiveness of VSV relies on the quality of visual cues extracted by the LVLM's vision encoder.
The current implementation focuses on single-round tasks and may require adaptation for interactive scenarios like visual dialogue.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) can reason effectively over both textual and visual inputs, but they tend to hallucinate syntactically coherent yet visually ungrounded contents. In this paper, we investigate the internal dynamics of hallucination by examining the tokens logits ranking throughout the generation process, revealing three key patterns in how LVLMs process information: (1) gradual visual information loss - visually grounded tokens gradually become less favored throughout generation, and (2) early excitation - semantically meaningful tokens achieve peak activation in the layers earlier than the final layer. (3) hidden genuine information - visually grounded tokens though not being eventually decoded still retain relatively high rankings at inference. Based on these insights, we propose VISTA (Visual Information Steering with Token-logit Augmentation), a training-free inference-time intervention framework that reduces hallucination while promoting genuine information. VISTA works by combining two complementary approaches: reinforcing visual information in activation space and leveraging early layer activations to promote semantically meaningful decoding. Compared to existing methods, VISTA requires no external supervision and is applicable to various decoding strategies. Extensive experiments show that VISTA on average reduces hallucination by about 40% on evaluated open-ended generation task, and it consistently outperforms existing methods on four benchmarks across four architectures under three decoding strategies. Code is available at https://github.com/LzVv123456/VISTA.

papers.title: Interpreting Large Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse dictionary learning methods (Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations) be scaled and applied to interpret and control large text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: This work successfully scales Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) to a large text-to-image diffusion model (FLUX.1), demonstrating they can decompose residual stream activations into interpretable features and enable targeted steering of image generation.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations are effective methods for interpreting and steering large text-to-image diffusion models, with SAE features being particularly suitable for manipulating concrete semantic concepts in generated images.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and outperform MLP neurons on automated interpretability metrics.
ITDA achieves comparable interpretability to SAEs but tends to encode more abstract visual attributes (colors, textures) while SAE features capture more concrete objects.
Steering image generation via SAE feature activation addition is effective but constrained, requiring the initial prompt to be semantically related to the steered feature.
The residual stream activations in FLUX.1 are highly anisotropic, necessitating PCA whitening for effective SAE training to avoid a high proportion of dead features.
ITDA generally achieves superior reconstruction performance compared to SAEs at similar dictionary sizes.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability (autointerp) metrics do not distinguish between abstract visual properties and manipulable semantic concepts, a qualitative difference observed between ITDA and SAE features.
Steering with SAE features is constrained and only effective when the initial image prompt is semantically related to the feature being added.
The autointerp pipeline may have biases, such as picking up on simple image characteristics like color rather than the intended semantic feature.
future_direction: Applying SAEs to vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation (sparse probing).
Adapting the SAE encoder architecture to incorporate spatial inductive bias (e.g., convolutional layers) for image data.
Improving steering techniques, potentially by making the process more similar to finetuning or otherwise more aware of steering effects.
Investigating shared features between the text and image streams of the multimodal DiT architecture.
Comparing the two FLUX.1 variants (Dev and Schnell) using methods like crosscoders to find corresponding or unique features.
Investigating biases specific to the automated interpretability pipeline.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders are a promising new approach for decomposing language model activations for interpretation and control. They have been applied successfully to vision transformer image encoders and to small-scale diffusion models. Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) is a recently proposed variant of dictionary learning that takes the dictionary to be a set of data points from the activation distribution and reconstructs them with gradient pursuit. We apply Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and ITDA to a large text-to-image diffusion model, Flux 1, and consider the interpretability of embeddings of both by introducing a visual automated interpretation pipeline. We find that SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and beat MLP neurons on interpretability. We are able to use SAE features to steer image generation through activation addition. We find that ITDA has comparable interpretability to SAEs.

papers.title: Denoising autoencoder with modulated lateral connections learns invariant representations of natural images
papers.research_question: How do lateral connections in denoising autoencoders affect the learning of invariant representations? Specifically, do modulated lateral connections allow higher layers to focus on invariant features and improve denoising performance?
papers.core_contribution: Modulated lateral connections in denoising autoencoders allow higher layers to focus on invariant representations, improving denoising performance and leading to diverse invariant poolings.
papers.conclusion: Modulated lateral connections enable denoising autoencoders to learn invariant representations and are compatible with supervised learning pipelines that include pooling operations.
papers.key_findings:
Modulated lateral connections improve denoising performance compared to additive lateral connections and no lateral connections.
Modulated lateral connections result in representations whose degree of invariance grows faster towards higher layers.
Modulated lateral connections support the formation of diverse invariant poolings.
The optimal layer size ratio (alpha) is small for modulated lateral connections, indicating a bottom-heavy structure.
Invariant neurons tend to have negative weights, leading to concave OR-like pooling operations.
future_direction: explicit bias towards invariances
sparse structure such as convolutional networks
dynamic models
papers.abstract: Suitable lateral connections between encoder and decoder are shown to allow higher layers of a denoising autoencoder (dAE) to focus on invariant representations. In regular autoencoders, detailed information needs to be carried through the highest layers but lateral connections from encoder to decoder relieve this pressure. It is shown that abstract invariant features can be translated to detailed reconstructions when invariant features are allowed to modulate the strength of the lateral connection. Three dAE structures with modulated and additive lateral connections, and without lateral connections were compared in experiments using real-world images. The experiments verify that adding modulated lateral connections to the model 1) improves the accuracy of the probability model for inputs, as measured by denoising performance; 2) results in representations whose degree of invariance grows faster towards the higher layers; and 3) supports the formation of diverse invariant poolings.

papers.title: Visual Sparse Steering: Improving Zero-shot Image Classification with Sparsity Guided Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can vision foundation models be steered at inference time without retraining or large labeled datasets, using sparse features from Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces VS2, a test-time method that uses sparse features from Sparse Autoencoders to steer vision foundation models, improving zero-shot image classification without retraining or contrastive data.
papers.conclusion: VS2 and its variants effectively steer vision foundation models using sparse features from Sparse Autoencoders, significantly improving zero-shot classification performance while retaining interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
VS2 consistently outperforms zero-shot CLIP and other baselines across multiple datasets and backbones without external data.
VS2++, a retrieval-augmented variant, achieves even larger gains when oracle positive/negative sets are available, but performance drops with noisy pseudo-labels.
Prototype-Aligned Sparse Steering (PASS) further improves performance by aligning SAE features with class prototypes during training, though gains are modest on fine-grained datasets.
Per-class analysis shows VS2 and VS2++ improve accuracy most on visually or taxonomically confusing categories, indicating disambiguation of fine-grained confusions.
The method is robust to hyperparameter variations and does not require tuning the backbone model.
papers.limitation:
VS2++ performance degrades when pseudo-labels are noisy (non-oracle cache), highlighting the need for better feature selection under weakly supervised retrieval.
Gains from prototype alignment (PASS) are modest on fine-grained datasets like CUB-200 and Tiny-ImageNet, suggesting classes sharing many features may require richer or multi-prototype guidance.
future_direction: Selecting appropriate prototypes or exploring multi-prototype guidance for better feature alignment.
Improving feature selection under weakly supervised retrieval scenarios.
papers.abstract: Steering vision foundation models at inference time without retraining or access to large labeled datasets is a desirable yet challenging objective, particularly in dynamic or resource-constrained settings. In this paper, we introduce Visual Sparse Steering (VS2), a lightweight, test-time method that guides vision models using steering vectors derived from sparse features learned by top-$k$ Sparse Autoencoders without requiring contrastive data. Specifically, VS2 surpasses zero-shot CLIP by 4.12% on CIFAR-100, 1.08% on CUB-200, and 1.84% on Tiny-ImageNet. We further propose VS2++, a retrieval-augmented variant that selectively amplifies relevant sparse features using pseudo-labeled neighbors at inference time. With oracle positive/negative sets, VS2++ achieves absolute top-1 gains over CLIP zero-shot of up to 21.44% on CIFAR-100, 7.08% on CUB-200, and 20.47% on Tiny-ImageNet. Interestingly, VS2 and VS2++ raise per-class accuracy by up to 25% and 38%, respectively, showing that sparse steering benefits specific classes by disambiguating visually or taxonomically proximate categories rather than providing a uniform boost. Finally, to better align the sparse features learned through the SAE reconstruction task with those relevant for downstream performance, we propose Prototype-Aligned Sparse Steering (PASS). By incorporating a prototype-alignment loss during SAE training, using labels only during training while remaining fully test-time unsupervised, PASS consistently, though modestly, outperforms VS2, achieving a 6.12% gain over VS2 only on CIFAR-100 with ViT-B/32.

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and share representations of morphosyntactic concepts (e.g., grammatical number, gender, tense) across typologically diverse languages?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models develop shared, causally relevant representations of abstract grammatical concepts across many languages, even when trained on imbalanced, English-centric data.
papers.conclusion: Large language models learn robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts, suggesting an internal 'lingua franca' of shared conceptual representations rather than language-specific encodings.
papers.key_findings:
A significant fraction of sparse autoencoder features encoding morphosyntactic concepts are shared across typologically diverse languages.
Ablating multilingual features significantly decreases classifier performance across languages, indicating models rely on shared representations.
Causal interventions on single multilingual features can selectively modify model behavior (e.g., in machine translation) with minimal side effects.
The identified multilingual features are human-interpretable and their sharing patterns are consistent across models with different training data balances (Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B).
The most massively multilingual features (shared across many languages) explain most of the probes' behavior, despite being a small subset.
papers.limitation:
Feature steering interventions require careful tuning of activation scales and can sometimes lead to degenerate or unexpected outputs.
There is a distinction between a model encoding a concept (as measured by probes) and using it during generation; some features causal for probes may not affect generation.
Human interpretation of features is likely biased and may not fully capture the model's internal concept spaces.
Sparse autoencoders may struggle to recover features that are encoded in a non-linear manner.
future_direction: Optimizing feature steering methods to avoid degenerate outputs and improve reliability.
Further investigating the distinction between concept representation and concept generation in models.
Exploring non-linear methods for feature discovery to capture more complex encodings.
papers.abstract: Jannik Brinkmann, Chris Wendler, Christian Bartelt, Aaron Mueller. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: One-Step is Enough: Sparse Autoencoders for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders learn interpretable features for text-to-image diffusion models, and do these features generalize across different denoising steps and model architectures?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs can learn interpretable features from one-step text-to-image diffusion models that generalize across steps and architectures, enabling causal intervention and revealing block specialization.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a promising approach for understanding and manipulating the internal mechanisms of text-to-image diffusion models, and one-step training is sufficient for learning features that generalize to multi-step models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on one-step SDXL Turbo generalize to 4-step SDXL Turbo and multi-step SDXL base model without additional training.
The learned features are interpretable and causally influence the image generation process.
Transformer blocks specialize into roles: up.0.0 for details, up.0.1 for style, and down.2.1 for composition.
RIEBench shows SAE features allow fine-grained image editing with fewer features compared to neuron interventions.
