The model learns to estimate the Elo rating (player skill) as a latent variable to improve next-character prediction, and this representation can also be probed.
Interventions using vectors derived from linear probes or contrastive activations can successfully edit the model's internal board state, causing it to play legal moves under a hypothetical modified board.
Adding a skill vector derived from contrastive activations to the model's MLP bias term can increase the model's win rate against Stockfish by up to 2.6 times, while subtracting it decreases performance.
The board state representation peaks in accuracy in the middle layers of the model, while the skill representation peaks in the final layers, suggesting parallel computation of board state and skill estimation.
papers.limitation:
The board state intervention success rate is 92%, indicating potential for improved intervention strategies.
Interventions can have unintended side effects, making the positions of other pieces less distinct.
The model's maximum input length of 1,023 characters limits the number of turns in a game.
Chess is a well-defined, rule-based system that does not capture the complexity and ambiguity present in less structured environments like natural language.
future_direction: Improving intervention strategies
Applying the techniques to natural language domains
Using the methods for applications like detecting and reducing hallucinations in LLMs
papers.abstract: Language models have shown unprecedented capabilities, sparking debate over the source of their performance. Is it merely the outcome of learning syntactic patterns and surface level statistics, or do they extract semantics and a world model from the text? Prior work by Li et al. investigated this by training a GPT model on synthetic, randomly generated Othello games and found that the model learned an internal representation of the board state. We extend this work into the more complex domain of chess, training on real games and investigating our model's internal representations using linear probes and contrastive activations. The model is given no a priori knowledge of the game and is solely trained on next character prediction, yet we find evidence of internal representations of board state. We validate these internal representations by using them to make interventions on the model's activations and edit its internal board state. Unlike Li et al's prior synthetic dataset approach, our analysis finds that the model also learns to estimate latent variables like player skill to better predict the next character. We derive a player skill vector and add it to the model, improving the model's win rate by up to 2.6 times.

papers.title: Interpretable and Steerable Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the interpretability and steerability of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) by incorporating user-specified concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE), a framework that prunes low-utility SAE neurons and augments the latent space with a concept bottleneck aligned to user-defined concepts, improving interpretability and steerability.
papers.conclusion: CB-SAE unifies sparse autoencoders with concept bottleneck models, enabling robust interpretation and control of vision representations across modalities and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE neurons have low interpretability or steerability, rendering them ineffective for downstream use.
SAEs often fail to represent user-specified concepts, limiting their practical utility.
CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% over SAE baselines across LVLMs and image generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) promise a unified approach for mechanistic interpretability, concept discovery, and model steering in LLMs and LVLMs. However, realizing this potential requires that the learned features be both interpretable and steerable. To that end, we introduce two new computationally inexpensive interpretability and steerability metrics and conduct a systematic analysis on LVLMs. Our analysis uncovers two observations; (i) a majority of SAE neurons exhibit either low interpretability or low steerability or both, rendering them ineffective for downstream use; and (ii) due to the unsupervised nature of SAEs, user-desired concepts are often absent in the learned dictionary, thus limiting their practical utility. To address these limitations, we propose Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE) - a novel post-hoc framework that prunes low-utility neurons and augments the latent space with a lightweight concept bottleneck aligned to a user-defined concept set. The resulting CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% across LVLMs and image generation tasks. We will make our code and model weights available.

papers.title: The Hidden Life of Tokens: Reducing Hallucination of Large Vision-Language Models via Visual Information Steering
papers.research_question: How does hallucination emerge and propagate internally during generation in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), and how can it be reduced via inference-time intervention?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces VISTA, a training-free inference-time intervention framework that reduces hallucination in LVLMs by reinforcing visual information in the activation space (via Visual Steering Vector) and leveraging early-layer semantic information (via Self-Logits Augmentation).
papers.conclusion: VISTA effectively reduces hallucination in LVLMs while preserving generation quality, establishing visual information steering as a promising direction for enhancing the reliability of multimodal AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Gradual visual information loss: visually grounded tokens become less favored as generation progresses.
Early excitation: semantically meaningful tokens achieve peak activation in layers earlier than the final layer.
Hidden genuine information: visually grounded tokens not decoded still retain relatively high rankings during inference.
VISTA reduces hallucination by about 40% on average in open-ended generation tasks.
VISTA outperforms existing methods across four benchmarks, four architectures, and three decoding strategies.
papers.limitation:
Optimal hyperparameter settings may vary across different architectures.
The effectiveness of VSV relies on the quality of visual cues extracted by the LVLM's vision encoder.
The current implementation focuses on single-round tasks and may require adaptation for interactive scenarios like visual dialogue.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) can reason effectively over both textual and visual inputs, but they tend to hallucinate syntactically coherent yet visually ungrounded contents. In this paper, we investigate the internal dynamics of hallucination by examining the tokens logits ranking throughout the generation process, revealing three key patterns in how LVLMs process information: (1) gradual visual information loss - visually grounded tokens gradually become less favored throughout generation, and (2) early excitation - semantically meaningful tokens achieve peak activation in the layers earlier than the final layer. (3) hidden genuine information - visually grounded tokens though not being eventually decoded still retain relatively high rankings at inference. Based on these insights, we propose VISTA (Visual Information Steering with Token-logit Augmentation), a training-free inference-time intervention framework that reduces hallucination while promoting genuine information. VISTA works by combining two complementary approaches: reinforcing visual information in activation space and leveraging early layer activations to promote semantically meaningful decoding. Compared to existing methods, VISTA requires no external supervision and is applicable to various decoding strategies. Extensive experiments show that VISTA on average reduces hallucination by about 40% on evaluated open-ended generation task, and it consistently outperforms existing methods on four benchmarks across four architectures under three decoding strategies. Code is available at https://github.com/LzVv123456/VISTA.

papers.title: Interpreting Large Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse dictionary learning methods (Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations) be scaled and applied to interpret and control large text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: This work successfully scales Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) to a large text-to-image diffusion model (FLUX.1), demonstrating they can decompose residual stream activations into interpretable features and enable targeted steering of image generation.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations are effective methods for interpreting and steering large text-to-image diffusion models, with SAE features being particularly suitable for manipulating concrete semantic concepts in generated images.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and outperform MLP neurons on automated interpretability metrics.
ITDA achieves comparable interpretability to SAEs but tends to encode more abstract visual attributes (colors, textures) while SAE features capture more concrete objects.
Steering image generation via SAE feature activation addition is effective but constrained, requiring the initial prompt to be semantically related to the steered feature.
The residual stream activations in FLUX.1 are highly anisotropic, necessitating PCA whitening for effective SAE training to avoid a high proportion of dead features.
ITDA generally achieves superior reconstruction performance compared to SAEs at similar dictionary sizes.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability (autointerp) metrics do not distinguish between abstract visual properties and manipulable semantic concepts, a qualitative difference observed between ITDA and SAE features.
Steering with SAE features is constrained and only effective when the initial image prompt is semantically related to the feature being added.
The autointerp pipeline may have biases, such as picking up on simple image characteristics like color rather than the intended semantic feature.
future_direction: Applying SAEs to vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation (sparse probing).
Adapting the SAE encoder architecture to incorporate spatial inductive bias (e.g., convolutional layers) for image data.
Improving steering techniques, potentially by making the process more similar to finetuning or otherwise more aware of steering effects.
Investigating shared features between the text and image streams of the multimodal DiT architecture.
Comparing the two FLUX.1 variants (Dev and Schnell) using methods like crosscoders to find corresponding or unique features.
Investigating biases specific to the automated interpretability pipeline.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders are a promising new approach for decomposing language model activations for interpretation and control. They have been applied successfully to vision transformer image encoders and to small-scale diffusion models. Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) is a recently proposed variant of dictionary learning that takes the dictionary to be a set of data points from the activation distribution and reconstructs them with gradient pursuit. We apply Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and ITDA to a large text-to-image diffusion model, Flux 1, and consider the interpretability of embeddings of both by introducing a visual automated interpretation pipeline. We find that SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and beat MLP neurons on interpretability. We are able to use SAE features to steer image generation through activation addition. We find that ITDA has comparable interpretability to SAEs.

papers.title: Denoising autoencoder with modulated lateral connections learns invariant representations of natural images
papers.research_question: How do lateral connections in denoising autoencoders affect the learning of invariant representations? Specifically, do modulated lateral connections allow higher layers to focus on invariant features and improve denoising performance?
papers.core_contribution: Modulated lateral connections in denoising autoencoders allow higher layers to focus on invariant representations, improving denoising performance and leading to diverse invariant poolings.
papers.conclusion: Modulated lateral connections enable denoising autoencoders to learn invariant representations and are compatible with supervised learning pipelines that include pooling operations.
papers.key_findings:
Modulated lateral connections improve denoising performance compared to additive lateral connections and no lateral connections.
Modulated lateral connections result in representations whose degree of invariance grows faster towards higher layers.
Modulated lateral connections support the formation of diverse invariant poolings.
The optimal layer size ratio (alpha) is small for modulated lateral connections, indicating a bottom-heavy structure.
Invariant neurons tend to have negative weights, leading to concave OR-like pooling operations.
future_direction: explicit bias towards invariances
sparse structure such as convolutional networks
dynamic models
papers.abstract: Suitable lateral connections between encoder and decoder are shown to allow higher layers of a denoising autoencoder (dAE) to focus on invariant representations. In regular autoencoders, detailed information needs to be carried through the highest layers but lateral connections from encoder to decoder relieve this pressure. It is shown that abstract invariant features can be translated to detailed reconstructions when invariant features are allowed to modulate the strength of the lateral connection. Three dAE structures with modulated and additive lateral connections, and without lateral connections were compared in experiments using real-world images. The experiments verify that adding modulated lateral connections to the model 1) improves the accuracy of the probability model for inputs, as measured by denoising performance; 2) results in representations whose degree of invariance grows faster towards the higher layers; and 3) supports the formation of diverse invariant poolings.

papers.title: Visual Sparse Steering: Improving Zero-shot Image Classification with Sparsity Guided Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can vision foundation models be steered at inference time without retraining or large labeled datasets, using sparse features from Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces VS2, a test-time method that uses sparse features from Sparse Autoencoders to steer vision foundation models, improving zero-shot image classification without retraining or contrastive data.
papers.conclusion: VS2 and its variants effectively steer vision foundation models using sparse features from Sparse Autoencoders, significantly improving zero-shot classification performance while retaining interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
VS2 consistently outperforms zero-shot CLIP and other baselines across multiple datasets and backbones without external data.
VS2++, a retrieval-augmented variant, achieves even larger gains when oracle positive/negative sets are available, but performance drops with noisy pseudo-labels.
Prototype-Aligned Sparse Steering (PASS) further improves performance by aligning SAE features with class prototypes during training, though gains are modest on fine-grained datasets.
Per-class analysis shows VS2 and VS2++ improve accuracy most on visually or taxonomically confusing categories, indicating disambiguation of fine-grained confusions.
The method is robust to hyperparameter variations and does not require tuning the backbone model.
papers.limitation:
VS2++ performance degrades when pseudo-labels are noisy (non-oracle cache), highlighting the need for better feature selection under weakly supervised retrieval.
Gains from prototype alignment (PASS) are modest on fine-grained datasets like CUB-200 and Tiny-ImageNet, suggesting classes sharing many features may require richer or multi-prototype guidance.
future_direction: Selecting appropriate prototypes or exploring multi-prototype guidance for better feature alignment.
Improving feature selection under weakly supervised retrieval scenarios.
papers.abstract: Steering vision foundation models at inference time without retraining or access to large labeled datasets is a desirable yet challenging objective, particularly in dynamic or resource-constrained settings. In this paper, we introduce Visual Sparse Steering (VS2), a lightweight, test-time method that guides vision models using steering vectors derived from sparse features learned by top-$k$ Sparse Autoencoders without requiring contrastive data. Specifically, VS2 surpasses zero-shot CLIP by 4.12% on CIFAR-100, 1.08% on CUB-200, and 1.84% on Tiny-ImageNet. We further propose VS2++, a retrieval-augmented variant that selectively amplifies relevant sparse features using pseudo-labeled neighbors at inference time. With oracle positive/negative sets, VS2++ achieves absolute top-1 gains over CLIP zero-shot of up to 21.44% on CIFAR-100, 7.08% on CUB-200, and 20.47% on Tiny-ImageNet. Interestingly, VS2 and VS2++ raise per-class accuracy by up to 25% and 38%, respectively, showing that sparse steering benefits specific classes by disambiguating visually or taxonomically proximate categories rather than providing a uniform boost. Finally, to better align the sparse features learned through the SAE reconstruction task with those relevant for downstream performance, we propose Prototype-Aligned Sparse Steering (PASS). By incorporating a prototype-alignment loss during SAE training, using labels only during training while remaining fully test-time unsupervised, PASS consistently, though modestly, outperforms VS2, achieving a 6.12% gain over VS2 only on CIFAR-100 with ViT-B/32.

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and share representations of morphosyntactic concepts (e.g., grammatical number, gender, tense) across typologically diverse languages?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models develop shared, causally relevant representations of abstract grammatical concepts across many languages, even when trained on imbalanced, English-centric data.
papers.conclusion: Large language models learn robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts, suggesting an internal 'lingua franca' of shared conceptual representations rather than language-specific encodings.
papers.key_findings:
A significant fraction of sparse autoencoder features encoding morphosyntactic concepts are shared across typologically diverse languages.
Ablating multilingual features significantly decreases classifier performance across languages, indicating models rely on shared representations.
Causal interventions on single multilingual features can selectively modify model behavior (e.g., in machine translation) with minimal side effects.
The identified multilingual features are human-interpretable and their sharing patterns are consistent across models with different training data balances (Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B).
The most massively multilingual features (shared across many languages) explain most of the probes' behavior, despite being a small subset.
papers.limitation:
Feature steering interventions require careful tuning of activation scales and can sometimes lead to degenerate or unexpected outputs.
There is a distinction between a model encoding a concept (as measured by probes) and using it during generation; some features causal for probes may not affect generation.
Human interpretation of features is likely biased and may not fully capture the model's internal concept spaces.
Sparse autoencoders may struggle to recover features that are encoded in a non-linear manner.
future_direction: Optimizing feature steering methods to avoid degenerate outputs and improve reliability.
Further investigating the distinction between concept representation and concept generation in models.
Exploring non-linear methods for feature discovery to capture more complex encodings.
papers.abstract: Jannik Brinkmann, Chris Wendler, Christian Bartelt, Aaron Mueller. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: One-Step is Enough: Sparse Autoencoders for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders learn interpretable features for text-to-image diffusion models, and do these features generalize across different denoising steps and model architectures?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs can learn interpretable features from one-step text-to-image diffusion models that generalize across steps and architectures, enabling causal intervention and revealing block specialization.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a promising approach for understanding and manipulating the internal mechanisms of text-to-image diffusion models, and one-step training is sufficient for learning features that generalize to multi-step models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on one-step SDXL Turbo generalize to 4-step SDXL Turbo and multi-step SDXL base model without additional training.
The learned features are interpretable and causally influence the image generation process.
Transformer blocks specialize into roles: up.0.0 for details, up.0.1 for style, and down.2.1 for composition.
RIEBench shows SAE features allow fine-grained image editing with fewer features compared to neuron interventions.
One-step training is sufficient for learning meaningful features applicable to multi-step diffusion models.
papers.limitation: The change pose task is hard to achieve with the current RIEBench setup.
future_direction: Improving feature selection strategies for delete interventions
Extending SAEs to other diffusion models
Using learned features for advanced image editing and control
papers.abstract: For large language models (LLMs), sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been shown to decompose intermediate representations that often are not interpretable directly into sparse sums of interpretable features, facilitating better control and subsequent analysis. However, similar analyses and approaches have been lacking for text-to-image models. We investigate the possibility of using SAEs to learn interpretable features for SDXL Turbo, a few-step text-to-image diffusion model. To this end, we train SAEs on the updates performed by transformer blocks within SDXL Turbo's denoising U-net in its 1-step setting. Interestingly, we find that they generalize to 4-step SDXL Turbo and even to the multi-step SDXL base model (i.e., a different model) without additional training. In addition, we show that their learned features are interpretable, causally influence the generation process, and reveal specialization among the blocks. We do so by creating RIEBench, a representation-based image editing benchmark, for editing images while they are generated by turning on and off individual SAE features. This allows us to track which transformer blocks' features are the most impactful depending on the edit category. Our work is the first investigation of SAEs for interpretability in text-to-image diffusion models and our results establish SAEs as a promising approach for understanding and manipulating the internal mechanisms of text-to-image models.

papers.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural network representations, and whether a new SAE architecture (MP-SAE) can better capture such structures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability. However, recent work has demonstrated phenomenology of model representations that lies outside the scope of this hypothesis, showing signatures of hierarchical, nonlinear, and multi-dimensional features. This raises the question: do SAEs represent features that possess structure at odds with their motivating hypothesis? If not, does avoiding this mismatch help identify said features and gain further insights into neural network representations? To answer these questions, we take a construction-based approach and re-contextualize the popular matching pursuits (MP) algorithm from sparse coding to design MP-SAE -- an SAE that unrolls its encoder into a sequence of residual-guided steps, allowing it to capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features. Comparing this architecture with existing SAEs on a mixture of synthetic and natural data settings, we show: (i) hierarchical concepts induce conditionally orthogonal features, which existing SAEs are unable to faithfully capture, and (ii) the nonlinear encoding step of MP-SAE recovers highly meaningful features, helping us unravel shared structure in the seemingly dichotomous representation spaces of different modalities in a vision-language model, hence demonstrating the assumption that useful features are solely linearly accessible is insufficient. We also show that the sequential encoder principle of MP-SAE affords an additional benefit of adaptive sparsity at inference time, which may be of independent interest. Overall, we argue our results provide credence to the idea that interpretability should begin with the phenomenology of representations, with methods emerging from assumptions that fit it.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success. To reveal the secrets behind the scene of these powerful models, we present VALUE (Vision-And-Language Understanding Evaluation), a set of meticulously designed probing tasks (e.g., Visual Coreference Resolution, Visual Relation Detection, Linguistic Probing Tasks) generalizable to standard pre-trained V+L models, aiming to decipher the inner workings of multimodal pre-training (e.g., the implicit knowledge garnered in individual attention heads, the inherent cross-modal alignment learned through contextualized multimodal embeddings). Through extensive analysis of each archetypal model architecture via these probing tasks, our key observations are: (i) Pre-trained models exhibit a propensity for attending over text rather than images during inference. (ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: The Effects of Invertibility on the Representational Complexity of Encoders in Variational Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How does the invertibility of the generative map affect the required complexity of the encoder in variational autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: If the generative map is strongly invertible, the encoder can have similar complexity (polynomial overhead); for non-invertible generative maps, under cryptographic assumptions, the encoder must be exponentially larger.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides theoretical support for the empirical wisdom that learning deep generative models is harder when data lies on a low-dimensional manifold.
papers.key_findings:
For strongly invertible generative maps, the encoder can be approximated by a deep latent Gaussian with polynomial overhead in parameters.
For non-invertible generative maps, assuming one-way functions exist, any encoder that approximates the posterior well must have exponential size.
The results provide theoretical support for the empirical observation that learning deep generative models is harder when data lies on a low-dimensional manifold.
papers.abstract: Training and using modern neural-network based latent-variable generative models (like Variational Autoencoders) often require simultaneously training a generative direction along with an inferential(encoding) direction, which approximates the posterior distribution over the latent variables. Thus, the question arises: how complex does the inferential model need to be, in order to be able to accurately model the posterior distribution of a given generative model? In this paper, we identify an important property of the generative map impacting the required size of the encoder. We show that if the generative map is "strongly invertible" (in a sense we suitably formalize), the inferential model need not be much more complex. Conversely, we prove that there exist non-invertible generative maps, for which the encoding direction needs to be exponentially larger (under standard assumptions in computational complexity). Importantly, we do not require the generative model to be layerwise invertible, which a lot of the related literature assumes and isn't satisfied by many architectures used in practice (e.g. convolution and pooling based networks). Thus, we provide theoretical support for the empirical wisdom that learning deep generative models is harder when data lies on a low-dimensional manifold.

papers.title: Does higher interpretability imply better utility? A Pairwise Analysis on Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does higher interpretability of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features imply better steering utility for large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds only a weak positive association between SAE feature interpretability and steering utility, and introduces a new feature selection criterion (∆Token Confidence) that significantly improves steering performance.
papers.conclusion: There is a significant divergence between SAE interpretability and steering utility, suggesting that prioritizing interpretability does not guarantee improved steering performance.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability shows a relatively weak positive association with steering utility (Kendall's τb ≈ 0.298).
∆Token Confidence effectively selects features with strong steering performance, improving steering score by 52.52% over the previous best method.
After selecting high-utility features with ∆Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes or becomes negative.
future_direction: Developing advanced post-training feature selection protocols or fundamentally new, utility-oriented SAE training paradigms.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to steer large language models (LLMs), based on the assumption that their interpretable features naturally enable effective model behavior steering. Yet, a fundamental question remains unanswered: does higher interpretability indeed imply better steering utility? To answer this question, we train 90 SAEs across three LLMs (Gemma-2-2B, Qwen-2.5-3B, Gemma-2-9B), spanning five architectures and six sparsity levels, and evaluate their interpretability and steering utility based on SAEBench (arXiv:2501.12345) and AxBench (arXiv:2502.23456) respectively, and perform a rank-agreement analysis via Kendall's rank coefficients (tau b). Our analysis reveals only a relatively weak positive association (tau b approx 0.298), indicating that interpretability is an insufficient proxy for steering performance. We conjecture the interpretability utility gap may stem from the selection of SAE features, as not all of them are equally effective for steering. To further find features that truly steer the behavior of LLMs, we propose a novel selection criterion called Delta Token Confidence, which measures how much amplifying a feature changes the next token distribution. We show that our method improves the steering performance of three LLMs by 52.52 percent compared to the current best output score based criterion (arXiv:2503.34567). Strikingly, after selecting features with high Delta Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes (tau b approx 0), and can even become negative. This further highlights the divergence between interpretability and utility for the most effective steering features.

papers.title: Letters of the Alphabet: Discovering Natural Feature Sets
papers.research_question: How do hidden layers in a simple neural network represent input features, and how can natural feature sets be derived from the data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how hidden node activations in a neural network can be visualized to understand feature representation and how natural feature sets can be discovered by grouping similar inputs.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide a step-by-step blueprint for how neural networks derive natural feature sets from data, offering insights into feature representation in hidden layers.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden nodes in the network activate to specific features like vertical and horizontal bars in letter representations.
Nodes 2 and 5 are activated strongly by most letters, indicating potential overfitting or redundancy.
Natural feature sets group similarly shaped letters, such as A and H, or B, R, and P.
Adding 10% noise did not improve generalization in the natural feature sets experiment.
Heatmap visualizations effectively show which input patterns contribute to hidden node activations.
papers.limitation:
Adding 10% noise did not help the hidden nodes generalize better as expected.
Deciphering and visualizing hidden node activations took a lot of time and explanation.
future_direction: Spend more time formatting visualizations to efficiently display hidden node activations for natural feature sets.
Use algorithms to automatically determine the ideal number of hidden nodes to speed up development.
papers.abstract: Deep learning networks find intricate features in large datasets using the backpropagation algorithm. This algorithm repeatedly adjusts the network connections.' weights and examining the "hidden" nodes behavior between the input and output layer provides better insight into how neural networks create feature representations. Experiments built on each other show that activity differences computed within a layer can guide learning. A simple neural network is used, which includes a data set comprised of the alphabet letters, where each letter forms 81 input nodes comprised of 0 and 1s and a single hidden layer and an output layer. The first experiment explains how the hidden layers in this simple neural network represent the input data's features. The second experiment attempts to reverse-engineer the neural network to find the alphabet's natural feature sets. As the network interprets features, we can understand how it derives the natural feature sets for a given data. This understanding is essential to delve deeper into deep generative models, such as Boltzmann machines. Deep generative models are a class of unsupervised deep learning algorithms. The primary function of deep generative models is to find the natural feature sets for a given data set.

papers.title: Enabling Local Editing in Diffusion Models by Joint and Individual Component Analysis
papers.research_question: How to achieve local image editing in diffusion models by factorizing the latent semantics of the denoising network into joint and individual components.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method for local image editing in diffusion models by decomposing the Jacobian of the denoising network into joint and individual components, enabling localized semantic manipulations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method enables localized semantic manipulation of real images using pre-trained diffusion models by factorizing latent subspaces, with discovered directions generalizing across images and outperforming previous methods.
papers.key_findings:
The method identifies semantic directions in the latent space that are localized to specific image regions, enabling fine-grained editing.
Decomposing the Jacobian into joint and individual components disentangles global and local variations, allowing for edits that affect only the region of interest.
The discovered latent directions generalize from a single reference image to other images, making the method suitable for plug-and-play applications.
The method produces edits with higher fidelity and better localization compared to existing state-of-the-art alternatives, as measured by FID, ID, and ROIR metrics.
future_direction: Explore the latent semantics of video diffusion models.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Diffusion Models (DMs) have led to significant progress in visual synthesis and editing tasks, establishing them as a strong competitor to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). However, the latent space of DMs is not as well understood as that of GANs. Recent research has focused on unsupervised semantic discovery in the latent space of DMs by leveraging the bottleneck layer of the denoising network, which has been shown to exhibit properties of a semantic latent space. However, these approaches are limited to discovering global attributes. In this paper we address, the challenge of local image manipulation in DMs and introduce an unsupervised method to factorize the latent semantics learned by the denoising network of pre-trained DMs. Given an arbitrary image and defined regions of interest, we utilize the Jacobian of the denoising network to establish a relation between the regions of interest and their corresponding subspaces in the latent space. Furthermore, we disentangle the joint and individual components of these subspaces to identify latent directions that enable local image manipulation. Once discovered, these directions can be applied to different images to produce semantically consistent edits, making our method suitable for practical applications. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that our method can produce semantic edits that are more localized and have better fidelity compared to the state-of-the-art.

papers.title: GrAInS: Gradient-based Attribution for Inference-Time Steering of LLMs and VLMs
papers.research_question: How to improve inference-time steering of LLMs and VLMs by using gradient-based attribution to identify influential tokens and construct targeted steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GRAINS, an inference-time steering method that uses gradient-based attribution to identify influential tokens and construct targeted steering vectors, improving alignment in LLMs and VLMs without weight updates.
papers.conclusion: GRAINS provides an effective, interpretable, and modular approach for inference-time steering of LLMs and VLMs, improving alignment while preserving general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
GRAINS improves accuracy on TruthfulQA by 13.22% with Llama-3.1-8B.
Reduces hallucination rates on MMHal-Bench from 0.624 to 0.514 with LLaVA-1.6-7B.
Improves alignment win rates on SPA-VL by 8.11%.
Preserves general capabilities on MMLU and MMMU with minimal performance drop.
Outperforms fine-tuning and other steering baselines across multiple tasks.
papers.abstract: Inference-time steering methods offer a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) by modifying internal activations at test time without updating model weights. However, most existing approaches rely on fixed, global intervention vectors, overlook the causal influence of individual input tokens, and fail to leverage informative gradients from the model's logits, particularly in multimodal settings where visual and textual inputs contribute unevenly. To address these limitations, we introduce GrAInS, an inference-time steering approach that operates across both language-only and vision-language models and tasks. GrAInS uses contrastive, gradient-based attribution via Integrated Gradients to identify the top-k most influential tokens, both positively and negatively attributed based on their contribution to preferred versus dispreferred outputs. These tokens are then used to construct directional steering vectors that capture semantic shifts from undesirable to desirable behavior. During inference, GrAInS adjusts hidden activations at transformer layers guided by token-level attribution signals, and normalizes activations to preserve representational scale. This enables fine-grained, interpretable, and modular control over model behavior, without retraining or auxiliary supervision. Empirically, GrAInS consistently outperforms both fine-tuning and existing steering baselines: it achieves a 13.22% accuracy gain on TruthfulQA using Llama-3.1-8B, reduces hallucination rates on MMHal-Bench from 0.624 to 0.514 with LLaVA-1.6-7B, and improves alignment win rates on SPA-VL by 8.11%, all while preserving the model's fluency and general capabilities.

papers.title: Extracting Unlearned Information from LLMs with Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Can activation steering be used to exactly retrieve unlearned information from LLMs, and under what conditions does it work?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes activation steering as a method for exact information retrieval from unlearned LLMs, demonstrating its effectiveness on broad topics like Harry Potter but limitations on narrow topics.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is effective for retrieving unlearned information in broad domains but has limitations for narrow domains, highlighting a vulnerability in current unlearning techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering can increase the correct answer frequency for unlearned information in broad domains (e.g., Harry Potter).
The method does not generalize well to narrow unlearning scenarios (e.g., TOFU and ROME).
The success of the method depends on the breadth of the unlearned subject, with broader topics having more conceptual links that can be restored.
papers.limitation:
The method fails for narrow unlearning settings (e.g., TOFU and ROME).
The global setting requires a dataset of questions, which is not easily applicable in real-world scenarios.
papers.abstract: An unintended consequence of the vast pretraining of Large Language Models (LLMs) is the verbatim memorization of fragments of their training data, which may contain sensitive or copyrighted information. In recent years, unlearning has emerged as a solution to effectively remove sensitive knowledge from models after training. Yet, recent work has shown that supposedly deleted information can still be extracted by malicious actors through various attacks. Still, current attacks retrieve sets of possible candidate generations and are unable to pinpoint the output that contains the actual target information. We propose activation steering as a method for exact information retrieval from unlearned LLMs. We introduce a novel approach to generating steering vectors, named Anonymized Activation Steering. Additionally, we develop a simple word frequency method to pinpoint the correct answer among a set of candidates when retrieving unlearned information. Our evaluation across multiple unlearning techniques and datasets demonstrates that activation steering successfully recovers general knowledge (e.g., widely known fictional characters) while revealing limitations in retrieving specific information (e.g., details about non-public individuals). Overall, our results demonstrate that exact information retrieval from unlearned models is possible, highlighting a severe vulnerability of current unlearning techniques.

papers.title: Revealing the Dark Secrets of BERT
papers.research_question: What are the common attention patterns in BERT, how do they change during fine-tuning, and how important are individual heads for task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT's attention heads exhibit redundant patterns, indicating overparametrization, and that selectively disabling heads can improve performance on GLUE tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that BERT can benefit from disabling attention heads due to redundancy in encoded information, and suggests model pruning as a future direction.
papers.key_findings:
Five common attention patterns (vertical, diagonal, vertical+diagonal, block, heterogeneous) are repeated across heads, with only the heterogeneous pattern potentially capturing linguistically meaningful information.
Two heads in pre-trained BERT show attention patterns correlated with FrameNet semantic relations, but these heads are not important for GLUE task performance.
Fine-tuning changes attention patterns primarily in the last two layers of BERT.
Disabling certain attention heads can improve performance on GLUE tasks, with gains of up to 3.2% absolute improvement.
BERT is overparametrized, with redundant information encoded across heads.
future_direction: Study self-attention patterns in different languages, especially verb-final and free-word-order languages.
Investigate model pruning and finding optimal sub-architectures to reduce redundancy.
papers.abstract: Olga Kovaleva, Alexey Romanov, Anna Rogers, Anna Rumshisky. Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and the 9th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (EMNLP-IJCNLP). 2019.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Steering Effectiveness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can the reliability of activation-based steering in LLMs be diagnosed using internal model signals such as entropy and KL divergence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that internal mechanistic signals (NBF and KL divergence) can predict steering effectiveness and introduces rotation-based steering as a stronger baseline for activation-based steering methods.
papers.conclusion: Internal mechanistic signals can predict steering effectiveness, and rotation-based steering provides a stronger baseline for activation-based steering methods, making steering a more measurable and predictable process.
papers.key_findings:
LLM judges (ChatGPT-4o-mini and Gemini-Flash-2.5) show substantial agreement in evaluating steering outputs after correcting for calibration bias.
Effective steering is characterized by structured entropy preservation (NBF) and coherent KL alignment across decoding steps.
Internal signals (NBF, KL, attention patterns) can predict steering quality with reasonable accuracy.
Rotation-based steering outperforms naive additive steering in terms of steering-coherence trade-off.
Attention patterns show a drop in confidence immediately after the intervention layer, correlating with coherence.
papers.limitation:
Limited conceptual coverage (only nine target concepts).
Focus on GEMMA model family, may not generalize to newer models.
Regression formulation requires further refinement.
Label noise from LLM-based judges and qualitative nature of tasks.
papers.abstract: Activation-based steering enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to exhibit targeted behaviors by intervening on intermediate activations without retraining. Despite its widespread use, the mechanistic factors that govern when steering succeeds or fails remain poorly understood, as prior work has relied primarily on black-box outputs or LLM-based judges. In this study, we investigate whether the reliability of steering can be diagnosed using internal model signals. We focus on two information-theoretic measures: the entropy-derived Normalized Branching Factor (NBF), and the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between steered activations and targeted concepts in the vocabulary space. We hypothesize that effective steering corresponds to structured entropy preservation and coherent KL alignment across decoding steps. Building on a reliability study demonstrating high inter-judge agreement between two architecturally distinct LLMs, we use LLM-generated annotations as ground truth and show that these mechanistic signals provide meaningful predictive power for identifying successful steering and estimating failure probability. We further introduce a stronger evaluation baseline for Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and Sparse Autoencoder-based steering, the two most widely adopted activation-steering methods.

papers.title: ExpertSteer: Intervening in LLMs through Expert Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we guide LLMs to follow desired behaviors during inference by leveraging external expert models for activation steering, overcoming limitations of existing methods that rely on the model itself?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EXPERTSTEER, a method that leverages external expert models to generate steering vectors for activation steering in LLMs, enabling effective knowledge transfer without updating model parameters.
papers.conclusion: EXPERTSTEER is an effective and efficient activation steering method that enables knowledge transfer from any expert model to arbitrary target LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
EXPERTSTEER outperforms existing activation steering methods across diverse tasks and models.
It works effectively in both same-family and cross-family model settings.
RFMs are more effective for feature extraction compared to linear methods like PCA and mean difference.
The choice of expert model is crucial for effective steering.
EXPERTSTEER is computationally efficient.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet guiding them to follow desired behaviours during inference remains a significant challenge. Activation steering offers a promising method to control the generation process of LLMs by modifying their internal activations. However, existing methods commonly intervene in the model's behaviour using steering vectors generated by the model itself, which constrains their effectiveness to that specific model and excludes the possibility of leveraging powerful external expert models for steering. To address these limitations, we propose ExpertSteer, a novel approach that leverages arbitrary specialized expert models to generate steering vectors, enabling intervention in any LLMs. ExpertSteer transfers the knowledge from an expert model to a target LLM through a cohesive four-step process: first aligning representation dimensions with auto-encoders to enable cross-model transfer, then identifying intervention layer pairs based on mutual information analysis, next generating steering vectors from the expert model using Recursive Feature Machines, and finally applying these vectors on the identified layers during inference to selectively guide the target LLM without updating model parameters. We conduct comprehensive experiments using three LLMs on 15 popular benchmarks across four distinct domains. Experiments demonstrate that ExpertSteer significantly outperforms established baselines across diverse tasks at minimal cost.

papers.title: DISCO: Disentangled Communication Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Is steering the query and value representation spaces within attention heads more effective for controlling LLM behavior than steering attention head outputs or other spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCO Steering, a method that injects steering vectors directly into the query and value spaces of attention heads, providing more granular control and superior performance over existing steering vector baselines.
papers.conclusion: Query and value spaces are powerful building blocks for steering vector methods, and DISCO provides an effective and flexible approach for controlling LLM behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Query and value spaces exhibit higher linear discriminability of concepts compared to attention head outputs.
DISCO Steering disentangles the strong Communication Steering baseline, allowing independent control of query and value steering magnitudes.
DISCO achieves the best performance in 13 out of 16 experiments across multiple datasets and models.
Steering query spaces dynamically re-weights attention, while steering value spaces directly adds to the head output.
The method is effective for promoting and suppressing behaviors like truthfulness, power-seeking, wealth-seeking, and corrigibility.
papers.limitation:
Requires a dataset of positive and negative examples for each concept.
Steering vectors are linear, which may not capture nonlinear concepts.
Could be misused for jailbreaks or generating inappropriate content.
future_direction: Extending DISCO to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder, multimodal).
Exploring nonlinear steering vectors.
Applying DISCO to more complex behaviors and real-world applications.
papers.abstract: A variety of recent methods guide large language model outputs via the inference-time addition of steering vectors to residual-stream or attention-head representations. In contrast, we propose to inject steering vectors directly into the query and value representation spaces within attention heads. We provide evidence that a greater portion of these spaces exhibit high linear discriminability of concepts --a key property motivating the use of steering vectors-- than attention head outputs. We analytically characterize the effect of our method, which we term DISentangled COmmunication (DISCO) Steering, on attention head outputs. Our analysis reveals that DISCO disentangles a strong but underutilized baseline, steering attention inputs, which implicitly modifies queries and values in a rigid manner. In contrast, DISCO's direct modulation of these components enables more granular control. We find that DISCO achieves superior performance over a number of steering vector baselines across multiple datasets on LLaMA 3.1 8B and Gemma 2 9B, with steering efficacy scoring up to 19.1% higher than the runner-up. Our results support the conclusion that the query and value spaces are powerful building blocks for steering vector methods.

papers.title: Local minimization of prediction errors drives learning of invariant object representations in a generative network model of visual perception
papers.research_question: How can a multilayered predictive coding network learn invariant object representations from sequences of transformed objects through the local minimization of prediction errors?
papers.core_contribution: A predictive coding network with local Hebbian learning can learn invariant object representations from sequences of transformed objects, reproducing hierarchical timescales and generative capabilities observed in biological visual systems.
papers.conclusion: Predictive coding networks trained on dynamic sequences with local Hebbian learning can learn invariant object representations and generative models, providing a biologically plausible framework for visual perception.
papers.key_findings:
The network learns invariant object representations in the highest area, as shown by block-diagonal structure in representational dissimilarity matrices.
The network develops a hierarchy of timescales, with higher areas showing slower decay of autocorrelation, matching experimental data from rat visual cortex.
The network can reconstruct objects from partially occluded inputs via top-down predictions.
Error neurons decorrelate faster than representation neurons in higher areas, a novel prediction of the model.
The model outperforms static training and other self-supervised methods in decoding accuracy across various transformations.
papers.limitation:
The model is a simplification of biological cortex and does not account for all aspects of vision, such as dorsal stream functions.
The training requires repeated presentation of sequences, which may be achieved by replay mechanisms in the brain but is an assumption.
future_direction: Extend the model to more complex transformations and natural scenes.
Incorporate dorsal stream functions for action and spatial processing.
Test the prediction about faster decorrelation of error neurons experimentally.
papers.abstract: The ventral visual processing hierarchy of the cortex needs to fulfill at least two key functions: perceived objects must be mapped to high-level representations invariantly of the precise viewing conditions, and a generative model must be learned that allows, for instance, to fill in occluded information guided by visual experience. Here, we show how a multilayered predictive coding network can learn to recognize objects from the bottom up and to generate specific representations via a top-down pathway through a single learning rule: the local minimization of prediction errors. Trained on sequences of continuously transformed objects, neurons in the highest network area become tuned to object identity invariant of precise position, comparable to inferotemporal neurons in macaques. Drawing on this, the dynamic properties of invariant object representations reproduce experimentally observed hierarchies of timescales from low to high levels of the ventral processing stream. The predicted faster decorrelation of error-neuron activity compared to representation neurons is of relevance for the experimental search for neural correlates of prediction errors. Lastly, the generative capacity of the network is confirmed by reconstructing specific object images, robust to partial occlusion of the inputs. By learning invariance from temporal continuity within a generative model, the approach generalizes the predictive coding framework to dynamic inputs in a more biologically plausible way than self-supervised networks with non-local error-backpropagation. This was achieved simply by shifting the training paradigm to dynamic inputs, with little change in architecture and learning rule from static input-reconstructing Hebbian predictive coding networks.

papers.title: Exploring the Role of BERT Token Representations to Explain Sentence Probing Results
papers.research_question: What role do specific token representations play in BERT's ability to encode linguistic features and explain probing results?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes linguistic features in specific token representations, and gradient-based attribution can reveal these subspaces to explain probing performance.
papers.conclusion: BERT's token representations encode specific linguistic knowledge, and attribution methods provide insights into probing results, revealing distinct subspaces for different features.
papers.key_findings:
Sentence-ending tokens retain positional information in higher layers.
The ##s token encodes both noun number and verb tense information, and BERT separates these usages into distinct subspaces.
In bi-gram shift tasks, inverted tokens have higher attribution scores, and abnormalities are encoded in their representations.
In coordination inversion, coordinators like 'and' and 'but' play a key role, and their representations change significantly.
Attribution patterns are consistent even with less training data, indicating that knowledge is well-encoded in representations.
future_direction: Investigate how subspaces evolve during fine-tuning
Check if behaviors are affected by different training objectives
Use token-level analysis for model efficiency
papers.abstract: Several studies have been carried out on revealing linguistic features captured by BERT. This is usually achieved by training a diagnostic classifier on the representations obtained from different layers of BERT. The subsequent classification accuracy is then interpreted as the ability of the model in encoding the corresponding linguistic property. Despite providing insights, these studies have left out the potential role of token representations. In this paper, we provide a more in-depth analysis on the representation space of BERT in search for distinct and meaningful subspaces that can explain the reasons behind these probing results. Based on a set of probing tasks and with the help of attribution methods we show that BERT tends to encode meaningful knowledge in specific token representations (which are often ignored in standard classification setups), allowing the model to detect syntactic and semantic abnormalities, and to distinctively separate grammatical number and tense subspaces. 1

papers.title: Brain2GAN: Feature-disentangled neural encoding and decoding of visual perception in the primate brain
papers.research_question: How do feature-disentangled latent representations of generative models align with neural representations in the primate visual cortex, and can they be used for accurate neural decoding (reconstruction of visual stimuli from brain activity)?
papers.core_contribution: Feature-disentangled w-latents of GANs (StyleGAN) align better with high-level neural representations in the primate visual cortex than other latent representations (z-latents, CLIP-latents) and enable state-of-the-art reconstruction of visual stimuli from brain activity.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates the importance of feature disentanglement in explaining high-level neural representations and shows that unsupervised generative models like StyleGAN can serve as effective models for neural coding, with implications for neuroprosthetics and brain-computer interfaces.
papers.key_findings:
w-latents of StyleGAN outperform z-latents and CLIP-latents in predicting neural responses in high-level visual areas (IT cortex).
Neural decoding using w-latents results in high-fidelity reconstructions of both face and natural images from multi-unit activity.
The alignment between w-latents and neural representations suggests a shared encoding principle for visual phenomena, despite the GAN never being trained on neural data.
Time-based decoding reveals the temporal dynamics of information processing across visual areas V1, V4, and IT.
Linear operations applied to decoded w-latents (e.g., interpolation, arithmetic) yield semantically meaningful transformations in the reconstructed images.
papers.limitation: The study used a passive fixation task, which may not reflect natural vision where eye movements and attention play a role.
future_direction: Applying the method to more complex tasks and naturalistic settings.
Integrating the approach with other generative models and neural recording modalities.
Exploring the use of the method for clinical applications such as visual neuroprosthetics.
papers.abstract: A challenging goal of neural coding is to characterize the neural representations underlying visual perception. To this end, multi-unit activity (MUA) of macaque visual cortex was recorded in a passive fixation task upon presentation of faces and natural images. We analyzed the relationship between MUA and latent representations of state-of-the-art deep generative models, including the conventional and feature-disentangled representations of generative adversarial networks (GANs) (i.e., z- and w-latents of StyleGAN, respectively) and language-contrastive representations of latent diffusion networks (i.e., CLIP-latents of Stable Diffusion). A mass univariate neural encoding analysis of the latent representations showed that feature-disentangled w representations outperform both z and CLIP representations in explaining neural responses. Further, w-latent features were found to be positioned at the higher end of the complexity gradient which indicates that they capture visual information relevant to high-level neural activity. Subsequently, a multivariate neural decoding analysis of the feature-disentangled representations resulted in state-of-the-art spatiotemporal reconstructions of visual perception. Taken together, our results not only highlight the important role of feature-disentanglement in shaping high-level neural representations underlying visual perception but also serve as an important benchmark for the future of neural coding.

papers.title: Transfer Learning and Deep Domain Adaptation
papers.abstract: Transfer learning is an emerging technique in machine learning, by which we can solve a new task with the knowledge obtained from an old task in order to address the lack of labeled data. In particular deep domain adaptation (a branch of transfer learning) gets the most attention in recently published articles. The intuition behind this is that deep neural networks usually have a large capacity to learn representation from one dataset and part of the information can be further used for a new task. In this research, we firstly present the complete scenarios of transfer learning according to the domains and tasks. Secondly, we conduct a comprehensive survey related to deep domain adaptation and categorize the recent advances into three types based on implementing approaches: fine-tuning networks, adversarial domain adaptation, and sample-reconstruction approaches. Thirdly, we discuss the details of these methods and introduce some typical real-world applications. Finally, we conclude our work and explore some potential issues to be further addressed.

papers.title: AptSim2Real: Approximately-Paired Sim-to-Real Image Translation
papers.abstract: Advancements in graphics technology has increased the use of simulated data for training machine learning models. However, the simulated data often differs from real-world data, creating a distribution gap that can decrease the efficacy of models trained on simulation data in real-world applications. To mitigate this gap, sim-to-real domain transfer modifies simulated images to better match real-world data, enabling the effective use of simulation data in model training. Sim-to-real transfer utilizes image translation methods, which are divided into two main categories: paired and unpaired image-to-image translation. Paired image translation requires a perfect pixel match, making it difficult to apply in practice due to the lack of pixel-wise correspondence between simulation and real-world data. Unpaired image translation, while more suitable for sim-to-real transfer, is still challenging to learn for complex natural scenes. To address these challenges, we propose a third category: approximately-paired sim-to-real translation, where the source and target images do not need to be exactly paired. Our approximately-paired method, AptSim2Real, exploits the fact that simulators can generate scenes loosely resembling real-world scenes in terms of lighting, environment, and composition. Our novel training strategy results in significant qualitative and quantitative improvements, with up to a 24% improvement in FID score compared to the state-of-the-art unpaired image-translation methods.

papers.title: Syn2Real: A New Benchmark forSynthetic-to-Real Visual Domain Adaptation
papers.abstract: Unsupervised transfer of object recognition models from synthetic to real data is an important problem with many potential applications. The challenge is how to "adapt" a model trained on simulated images so that it performs well on real-world data without any additional supervision. Unfortunately, current benchmarks for this problem are limited in size and task diversity. In this paper, we present a new large-scale benchmark called Syn2Real, which consists of a synthetic domain rendered from 3D object models and two real-image domains containing the same object categories. We define three related tasks on this benchmark: closed-set object classification, open-set object classification, and object detection. Our evaluation of multiple state-of-the-art methods reveals a large gap in adaptation performance between the easier closed-set classification task and the more difficult open-set and detection tasks. We conclude that developing adaptation methods that work well across all three tasks presents a significant future challenge for syn2real domain transfer.

papers.title: DIRL: Domain-Invariant Representation Learning for Sim-to-Real Transfer
papers.abstract: Generating large-scale synthetic data in simulation is a feasible alternative to collecting/labelling real data for training vision-based deep learning models, albeit the modelling inaccuracies do not generalize to the physical world. In this paper, we present a domain-invariant representation learning (DIRL) algorithm to adapt deep models to the physical environment with a small amount of real data. Existing approaches that only mitigate the covariate shift by aligning the marginal distributions across the domains and assume the conditional distributions to be domain-invariant can lead to ambiguous transfer in real scenarios. We propose to jointly align the marginal (input domains) and the conditional (output labels) distributions to mitigate the covariate and the conditional shift across the domains with adversarial learning, and combine it with a triplet distribution loss to make the conditional distributions disjoint in the shared feature space. Experiments on digit domains yield state-of-the-art performance on challenging benchmarks, while sim-to-real transfer of object recognition for vision-based decluttering with a mobile robot improves from 26.8 % to 91.0 %, resulting in 86.5 % grasping accuracy of a wide variety of objects. Code and supplementary details are available at https://sites.google.com/view/dirl

papers.title: Sensor Transfer: Learning Optimal Sensor Effect Image Augmentation for\n Sim-to-Real Domain Adaptation
papers.abstract:
Performance on benchmark datasets has drastically improved with advances in
deep learning. Still, cross-dataset generalization performance remains
relatively low due to the domain shift that can occur between two different
datasets. This domain shift is especially exaggerated between synthetic and
real datasets. Significant research has been done to reduce this gap,
specifically via modeling variation in the spatial layout of a scene, such as
occlusions, and scene environmental factors, such as time of day and weather
effects. However, few works have addressed modeling the variation in the sensor
domain as a means of reducing the synthetic to real domain gap. The camera or
